introduction-the-grep-dead-end.core: Even structured logs fail if every team names things differently: userId, user_id, uid, customer.id. Queries then have to know every variant, dashboards break, and correlation across services is guesswork. Semantic logging goes further than JSON. Logs are typed events with an agreed schema and meaning (event names, field names, types, units), so they can be queried like a database across the whole organisation.

first_principles.problem: Finding all failed logins across 30 services needs a query listing seven different field names for 'user'.
truths: Structure without shared meaning is fragmented.

analogy.title: Every department using its own spreadsheet columns
analogy.story: Combining them is painful until everyone uses the same template.
analogy.breaks: Spreadsheets can be fixed by hand; logs at scale need automation.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One query works for every service.

check.q: Why are structured logs alone not enough for organisation-wide querying?
check.a: Different teams use different field names, types and units, so queries must account for every variant.

schema-discipline-the-semantic-part.core: Schema discipline means a documented, versioned catalogue of event types (payment.authorized, user.login.failed), each with required and optional fields, types, units and allowed values. Reuse namespaced common fields (service.name, user.id, http.response.status_code, error.type) from OTel semantic conventions or the Elastic Common Schema. Changes follow a versioning policy, and pipelines validate events against the schema.

first_principles.problem: A team changes a field from int to string, and every dashboard and alert using it silently breaks.

analogy.title: A standard form with defined boxes
analogy.story: Each box has a label, format and meaning; changing a box needs a new form version.
analogy.breaks: Paper forms are hard to change; schemas change easily, so discipline matters.

check.q: Why include units in field names like amount_minor or duration_ms?
check.a: It removes ambiguity about scale so consumers don't misinterpret values.

implementing-semantic-logging.core: Make the right thing easy: provide a shared logging library or wrapper per language with typed event helpers (log_payment_declined(payment, reason)) that set event.name and required fields automatically, inject common context (service, version, trace), generate code from the schema catalogue, and add CI linting that flags ad-hoc fields. Migrate gradually, mapping legacy fields in the pipeline.

first_principles.problem: Teams agree on a schema document, but six months later half the services ignore it.

analogy.title: Pre-printed forms instead of instructions
analogy.story: Give people the form with boxes already labelled, not a memo describing what to write.
analogy.breaks: Forms can't be skipped; ad-hoc logs still can, hence linting.

code.text:
# generated from events/payment.declined/v2
def payment_declined(log, *, payment_id: str, amount_minor: int, currency: str, error_type: str):
    log.warning("payment.declined",
                **{"event.name": "payment.declined", "payment.id": payment_id,
                   "payment.amount_minor": amount_minor, "payment.currency": currency,
                   "error.type": error_type})

payment_declined(log, payment_id=p.id, amount_minor=4999, currency="USD", error_type="card_declined")

check.q: What's the most effective way to get teams to follow a log schema?
check.a: Provide shared libraries with typed helpers (ideally generated from the schema) so compliance is the easy default, backed by CI linting.

context-propagation-and-log-correlation.core: Semantic events become powerful when they carry correlation context: trace_id and span_id to link to traces; business keys (order.id, payment.id, tenant.id) to follow an entity across services and asynchronous flows; and baggage for selected keys propagated through calls. Propagate context through HTTP, gRPC, queue message headers and background jobs, so an order's whole lifecycle can be reconstructed.

first_principles.problem: An order's events in checkout, payments and fulfilment can't be tied together because asynchronous queue consumers lose context.
truths: Async boundaries drop context by default.

analogy.title: A case file number on every document
analogy.story: Every department stamps the case number, so the full history can be assembled later.
analogy.breaks: Paper files don't lose stamps; async code loses context unless coded.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Order lifecycle traceable across async hops.

code.text:
from opentelemetry.propagate import inject, extract
# producer
headers = {}
inject(headers)
producer.send("orders", value=evt, headers=[(k, v.encode()) for k, v in headers.items()])
# consumer
ctx = extract({k: v.decode() for k, v in msg.headers})
with tracer.start_as_current_span("fulfil_order", context=ctx):
    log.info("order.fulfilment.started", **{"order.id": evt["order_id"]})

check.q: Why include business keys like order.id in addition to trace_id?
check.a: An entity's lifecycle may span multiple traces (async, retries, days), and business keys tie all its events together.

the-power-of-querying.core: With consistent semantic events, logs become an analytics dataset. You can count declines by error.type and currency, compute conversion funnels from event sequences, find p95 duration_ms by tenant, or join logins and payment failures by user.id, all across every service with one query. Columnar backends (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Loki structured metadata, Honeycomb-style stores) make such queries fast.

first_principles.problem: Product asks 'which card error types increased after the release?' and engineering needs a week of ad-hoc parsing.

analogy.title: A well-kept database instead of a pile of notes
analogy.story: Ask any new question with a query instead of re-reading every note.
analogy.breaks: Databases have strict schemas; event stores tolerate evolution with discipline.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Answer in seconds: 'fraud_suspected' tripled in EUR.

code.text:
SELECT error_type, currency, count() AS declines
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'payment.declined'
  AND timestamp >= now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  AND service_version = '2.4.0'
GROUP BY error_type, currency
ORDER BY declines DESC
LIMIT 10;

check.q: What makes cross-service log queries reliable?
check.a: Consistent event names and typed field names/units shared by all services (semantic schema).
